narrative:

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the second decile is well below the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted, signaling that your later academic performance was weaker than most successful applicants.

Your undergraduate GPA came next. At 2.60 it is noticeably lower than the 3.23 average of accepted students, which pulled the prediction toward failure, though this effect was smaller than the impact of your class rank.

Your high family income actually worked in your favor, nudging the outcome slightly toward passing. However, this positive influence was not large enough to overcome the academic signals.

In short, the model saw your relatively low class standing in year three and modest college grades as the dominant reasons you were unlikely to pass the bar on the first try. To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record, perhaps by taking additional coursework, retaking the LSAT to raise your score from 32, or gaining targeted bar-prep experience before reapplying. These steps can directly address the areas that most affected your current prediction.
